name: Sanlun (Madhyamaka)
desc:
The school is founded on the three treatises — the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]*, the *Śataśāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* — and belongs to the Prajñāpāramitā and [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] tradition. Its core is dependent origination and intrinsic emptiness, the middle way of the eight negations, the two truths, and non-attainment. Its ultimate aim is to realise the true reality of the middle way and enter the non-abiding nirvāṇa.

Its distinguishing feature is “refuting without establishing”: it demolishes layer by layer by way of the apophatic method (negation) and establishes no affirmative proposition, and therefore asserts no thesis of its own, saying only that “in refuting the false, the true is revealed.” In its doctrine of the two truths it holds to “the two truths as verbal teaching” — the two truths are the form of the Buddha's preaching, not the principle that is realised or the object that is contemplated.

Lineage: in India, Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250) → Āryadeva → transmitted to China through Kumārajīva (401) → Sengquan of Sheshan and Falang of Xinghuang → Jizang (549–623), who brought it to completion.

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: The fundamental basis for the [[two_truths|two truths]] and the middle way of the eight negations.

src.t: Jizang, *Erdi Yi* (Meaning of the Two Truths), *Dasheng Xuanlun* (Profound Discourse on the Mahāyāna), and *Sanlun Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Three Treatises)
src.q: The school's doctrine of the [[debate_two_truths|two truths as verbal teaching]] and of refuting the false to reveal the true.

tt.fix: establishment of the school in China: Sui–Tang, brought to completion by Jizang (549–623)
tt.trans: translated by Kumārajīva under the Yao Qin (401–409): the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the *Śataśāstra*, and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, from which the name “three treatises” derives

name: The Eight Negations
aka: middle way of the eight negations
desc:
Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, [[not_one_not_diff|neither one nor different]], neither coming nor going (Kumārajīva renders it “neither coming nor departing”). The middle way is revealed by way of negation (the apophatic method), avoiding any extreme.

The eight negations come from the salutation verse at the opening of the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]* and form the general outline of the whole work. Their structure is four pairs: arising and ceasing (existence and non-existence), permanence and annihilation, identity and difference, coming and going. The four pairs address respectively whether existence arises, whether time continues, whether identity holds, and whether motion is possible — that is, the four most basic types of attachment to “dharmas” both within Buddhism and among non-Buddhists.

The methodological significance of the eight negations is that they do not state the truth positively but reveal the middle way by showing that “this path does not lead through.” Madhyamaka is therefore called “refuting without establishing.” This method deeply influenced Tiantai, though Tiantai placed limits on its use and did not go to the Chan-style extreme.

src.q: “Neither arising nor ceasing, neither permanent nor annihilated, neither one nor different, neither coming nor departing. He who teaches dependent origination, who well extinguishes all conceptual proliferation.”

tt.trans: translated by Kumārajīva under the Yao Qin (*Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, c. 401–409)

name: Non-attainment and Non-abiding Nirvāṇa
desc:
Not grasping that any dharma is attainable; not abiding in birth-and-death (saṃsāra), nor abiding in [[nirvana|nirvāṇa]].

“Non-attainment” (anupalambha) is the practical principle of the [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] and Prajñāpāramitā traditions: if there is something attained, there is something grasped; if there is grasping, there can be no true liberation. Hence even “nirvāṇa” cannot be taken as an object to be attained.

Relation to Chan: the “non-abiding” of the Ox-head school and of Southern Chan shares this same source — the *Platform Sūtra* (Liuzu Tan Jing) takes “non-abiding as the root,” that is, not lingering over any dharma, which is structurally identical with “non-attainment.” The Sanlun school's “non-attainment” and Chan's “non-abiding” are thus the same principle expressed in different schools.

“Non-abiding nirvāṇa” is the Mahāyāna redefinition of nirvāṇa: unlike the hearers' “entering nirvāṇa and stopping there,” the bodhisattva, out of great compassion, does not abide in nirvāṇa, and, out of wisdom, does not abide in saṃsāra. This formulation turns nirvāṇa from an “endpoint” into a “state of non-attachment.”

src.t: *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (Da Bore Jing) and *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Dapin Banruo Jing)
src.q: “Non-attainment” as the fundamental mode of the practice of prajñā.
Not grasping the two extremes of existence and non-existence.

src.q: “Non-abiding is the root.”

name: Faxiang (Yogācāra)
desc:
The school is founded on the *[[doc_5|Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra]]*, the *[[doc_32|Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra]]*, and the *Cheng Weishi Lun*, and represents the transmission in China of the Indian Yogācāra tradition. Its core is the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, the transformation of the basis, and the four wisdoms. Its ultimate aim is to cut off the two obstructions (the affliction obstruction and the cognitive obstruction), realise the two emptinesses (the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas), transform consciousness into wisdom, and attain the three bodies of the Buddha.

Its distinguishing feature is the detailed analysis of dharma-characteristics: by means of precise classifications such as the five categories and one hundred dharmas and the fifty-one mental factors, it explains the constitution and causal relations of all dharmas, and is the most systematically philosophical of Buddhist systems. To the difficult problem of “non-self yet rebirth” it gives the most technical answer — ālaya-consciousness holds the seeds and receives perfuming, constantly turning like a torrent, neither permanent nor annihilated.

Lineage: in India, Asaṅga (c. 310–390) and Vasubandhu (c. 320–400) → Paramārtha (came to China in the 6th century; the Shelun masters) → Xuanzang (returned to China in 645; translated the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in 646–648; the *Cheng Weishi Lun* was completed in 659) → Kuiji.

Because it holds that among the “five lineages” there is one class of sentient beings who can never attain Buddhahood, it conflicts with the position of Tiantai, Huayan, and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* that “all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature.” Accordingly its doctrinal classification ranks the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* as the definitive meaning of the third period, while judging the *Lotus* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as provisional meaning prior to the “three periods” — this classificatory stance is precisely one of the greatest disagreements within Chinese Buddhist learning.

src.q: The scriptural source for the doctrine of the [[three_natures|three natures]] and of ālaya-consciousness.
The classification of the [[five_paths|five categories]] and one hundred dharmas, and the argument establishing ālaya-consciousness.
Compiled by conflating the commentaries of ten masters; the culminating work of [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] learning.

tt.fix: establishment of the school in China: Tang, Xuanzang (returned to China 645) and Kuiji (the *Cheng Weishi Lun* completed 659)
tt.trans: translated by Xuanzang in the Tang: the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* (647) and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (646–648); the *Cheng Weishi Lun* (659, Xuanzang’s composite translation of ten masters’ commentaries, recorded by Kuiji)

name: Tiantai
desc:
The school is founded on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Its core is [[one_mind_3000|three thousand realms in a single moment of mind]], the perfect interfusion of the three truths, threefold contemplation in one mind, and the [[six_identities|six identities]]. Its characteristic is to begin from the single moment of mind of the ordinary person, giving equal weight to doctrine and contemplation, with clear stages. Its ultimate aim is to open the Buddha's insight, perfectly realise true reality, and become the Buddha of the ultimate identity.

The structure of its thought is that “the perfect interfusion of the three truths” and “three thousand realms in a single moment of mind” support each other: the three truths explain the mode in which the mind is contemplated (empty, provisional, and middle at once), while three thousand realms in a single moment of mind explains the content of the mind (a single moment of mind suffices for the three thousand worlds). Their combination makes Tiantai the Chinese school most characterised by “perfect interfusion” — it does not divide phenomenon and noumenon into two levels, but says that every colour and every fragrance possesses the three thousand.

In doctrinal classification it takes the *Lotus Sūtra* as purely perfect and uniquely sublime, and the five periods and eight teachings rank the earlier sūtras as provisional teachings. Compared with Huayan: Huayan directly reveals the realm of the Buddha's fruit and is grand in scale; Tiantai begins from the single moment of mind of the ordinary person, with clear stages and strong practicability.

Lineage: Huiwen → Huisi → Zhiyi (538–597) → Guanding (who recorded and edited his works). Zhiyi's major works — the *Fahua Xuanyi*, the *Fahua Wenju*, and the *Mohe Zhiguan* — were all recorded by his disciple Guanding from his lectures.

src.q: The cardinal teaching of [[kaifozhijian|opening the Buddha's insight]] and of gathering the three into one.
The principal source for [[one_mind_3000|three thousand realms in a single moment of mind]], the perfect interfusion of the three truths, threefold contemplation in one mind, and the six identities.

src.q: The doctrinal classification of the [[wushi_bajiao|five periods and eight teachings]], and the one seal of true reality.

rel.four_foundations: an elaboration of the four establishments of mindfulness

name: Three Thousand Realms in a Single Moment of Mind
aka: three thousand worlds in one thought
desc:
A single moment of mind contains in full the three thousand worlds. The classic statement in fascicle 5 of the *[[doc_39|Mohe Zhiguan]]*: “Now, one mind contains the ten dharma-realms, and one dharma-realm in turn contains the ten dharma-realms, [making] a hundred dharma-realms; one realm contains thirty kinds of world, so a hundred dharma-realms contain three thousand kinds of world. These three thousand are in a single moment of mind: if there is no mind, that is all; but as soon as there is the slightest mind, it contains the three thousand.”

The calculation of the three thousand: the ten dharma-realms (the six ordinary realms plus the four noble realms) × the ten dharma-realms (each realm again containing the ten realms) = a hundred dharma-realms; a hundred dharma-realms × the ten suchnesses (characteristic, nature, substance, power, activity, cause, condition, effect, retribution, and the ultimate equality of beginning and end) = a thousand suchnesses; a thousand suchnesses × the three kinds of world (the world of the five aggregates, the world of sentient beings, and the world of the land) = the three thousand worlds.

The key lies in the relation between “a single moment” and “the three thousand.” The *Mohe Zhiguan* states explicitly: “It is not said that one mind comes first and all dharmas afterwards; nor is it said that all dharmas come first and one mind afterwards” — it is not that the mind generates the three thousand (vertically), nor that the mind contains the three thousand all at once (horizontally), but that “the mind alone is all dharmas, and all dharmas are the mind.” “The three thousand” is therefore a synonym for “all dharmas,” and one need not fixate on the number; its essential spirit is “inherent inclusion” — the ordinary person's present single moment of mind is already complete in possessing everything, with no need to seek outside.

The scriptural basis of the doctrine is the *[[doc_12|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]*, “Chapter on the Sovereignty of the Yāma Heaven Palace”: “Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction”; but “three thousand realms in a single moment of mind” itself is a contemplation unique to Tiantai.

src.q: “These three thousand are in a single moment of mind: if there is no mind, that is all; but as soon as there is the slightest mind, it contains the three thousand. It is not said that one mind comes first and all dharmas afterwards; nor is it said that all dharmas come first and one mind afterwards.”

src.t: Zhiyi, *Fahua Xuanyi* (Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuanyi), fascicle 2
src.q: “One who roams in mind through the dharma-realm contemplates how, when sense faculty and sense object stand opposed and a single moment of mind arises, it necessarily belongs to one of the ten realms; and belonging to one realm, it possesses the hundred realms and thousand dharmas, all of them fully complete within that single moment.”

src.t: *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, “Chapter on the Sovereignty of the Yāma Heaven Palace”
src.q: “Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings — these three are without distinction” — the scriptural basis for [[one_mind_3000|three thousand realms in a single moment of mind]].

tt.trans: spoken by Zhiyi, recorded by Guanding; the Tang monk Zhanran (711–782) wrote the *Fuxing* commentary

name: Perfect Interfusion of the Three Truths and Threefold Contemplation in One Mind
aka: perfect interfusion of the three truths
round fusion of the three truths
desc:
The three truths — emptiness, the provisional, and the middle — are not three successive stages but are perfectly illumined at once within one mind.

The scriptural basis for the three truths is the *[[doc_30|Mūlamadhyamakakārikā]]*, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”: “Whatever dharma arises from causes and conditions, I declare to be emptiness; it is also a provisional name, and is also called the meaning of the middle way.” The three phrases are the three truths of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Zhiyi's crucial treatment is “the mutual identity of the three truths”: the three — emptiness, provisional, middle — are “neither one nor three, yet one and yet three” — not three independent truths, but the simultaneous presentation of the same true reality from different angles.

“Threefold contemplation in one mind” is the corresponding contemplation: within one mind to contemplate emptiness, the provisional, and the middle simultaneously, without having to cultivate the three contemplations in stages. This stands in contrast to the “successive threefold contemplation” of the distinct teaching, and is the mark by which Tiantai judges the “perfect teaching.”

The relation of the three truths to the [[two_truths|two truths]]: the three truths are opened out from the two truths, and the three truths are the two truths — because the “middle” is not a third truth apart from the two truths, but the perfectly interfused aspect of the two truths. Tiantai therefore says, “the two truths open into the three truths, and the three truths are the two truths.”

Comparison with the Sanlun school: Sanlun discusses the middle way on the basis of the “eight negations” in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and sets it forth in conjunction with the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional; Tiantai, on the other hand, establishes the perfectly interfused three truths on the basis of the verse in the “Examination of the Four Noble Truths” chapter, so that Tiantai's view of the middle way carries more of a sense of “the perfectly interfused phenomenal realm” — “empty, provisional, and middle at once” affirms at the same time the validity of provisional names.

src.t: *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* (Zhong lun), fascicle 4, “Examination of the Four Noble Truths”
src.q: “Whatever dharma arises from causes and conditions, I declare to be emptiness; it is also a provisional name, and is also called the meaning of the middle way.”

name: The Six Identities

src.q: “The six identities: identity in principle, identity in name, identity in contemplative practice, identity in resemblance, identity in partial truth, and ultimate identity. These six identities begin with the ordinary and end with the sage; because they begin with the ordinary, doubt and timidity are removed; because they end with the sage, arrogant conceit is removed.”
“If one wishes to escape poverty, one should diligently practise the threefold contemplation; if one wishes to escape overweening pride, one should hear the six identities.”

name: Opening the Buddha's Insight
desc:
The cardinal teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra*: opening, showing, awakening to, and entering the Buddha's insight.

The sūtra says that the sole great cause for the Buddha's appearance in the world is to lead sentient beings to “open the Buddha's insight, show the Buddha's insight, awaken to the Buddha's insight, and enter the Buddha's insight.” Tiantai takes this as the reason for judging the *Lotus* to be purely perfect — the *Lotus* sets forth no expedient device apart from opening the provisional to reveal the real, but speaks only of the Buddha's true intent.

“Opening” has a double meaning: first, “opening away,” that is, removing sentient beings' attachment to provisional teachings; second, “opening up,” that is, revealing the Buddha's insight that is inherently possessed. “Opening the Buddha's insight” therefore corresponds structurally to “all sentient beings possess the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]]”: the insight is not added from outside but is inherently possessed and obscured.

Relation to the “[[six_identities|six identities]]”: “opening the Buddha's insight” is the cardinal teaching of the doctrinal classification, while the “six identities” are the stages of practice; the former explains the nature of the goal, the latter the position of attainment.

src.q: “The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely for the sake of one great cause ... wishing to lead sentient beings to [[kaifozhijian|open the Buddha's insight]], show the Buddha's insight, awaken to the Buddha's insight, and enter the Buddha's insight.”

tt.fix: Zhiyi took it as the cardinal teaching by which the *Lotus* is judged purely perfect
tt.trans: the *Lotus Sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva under the Yao Qin (406)

name: Huayan
desc:
The school is founded on the *[[doc_12|Avataṃsaka Sūtra]]*. Its core is the [[one_true_dharmadhatu|one true dharma-realm]], dharmadhātu dependent origination, the four dharma-realms, the ten mysterious gates, and the six characteristics in mutual interfusion. Its characteristic is to reveal directly the realm of the Buddha's fruit, teaching the non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon. Its ultimate aim is to realise and enter the one true dharma-realm and become Vairocana.

Its theoretical centre of gravity is “dharmadhātu dependent origination”: all dharmas are mutually dependent in origination, mutually identical and mutually interpenetrating; one is all and all is one. This shares a name with the “dependent origination” of the Āgamas but belongs to a different level — the Āgama dependent origination explains how the round of birth-and-death comes about, while Huayan's dharmadhātu dependent origination explains how, in the vision of one who has already become Buddha, all dharmas mutually contain one another.

In doctrinal classification it takes the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as “the one vehicle of the distinct teaching,” and the five teachings and ten schools rank the various schools at different levels. Compared with Tiantai's “beginning from the ordinary person's single moment of mind,” Huayan “directly reveals the realm of the Buddha's fruit,” and is therefore grand in scale but less practicable in its stages — which also explains why Tiantai received greater emphasis in practice.

Lineage: Dushun (the *Fajie Guan Men*) → Zhiyan (the ten mysterious gates) → Fazang (643–712; the *Five Teachings Chapter* and the *Tanxuan Ji*) → Chengguan (the four dharma-realms; the *Huayan Shu Chao*) → Zongmi (the fifth patriarch).

src.q: The scriptural source for the [[one_true_dharmadhatu|one true dharma-realm]] and for the simile of Indra's net.

name: The One True Dharma-Realm
desc:
The totality of the dharma-realm, which encompasses all things and is without duality or distinction. “One” means unique and without a second; “true” means real and not false; “dharma-realm” means the universal aspect of all dharmas.

The one true dharma-realm is the ultimate goal of Huayan: it is not another layer of reality apart from phenomena, but all phenomena themselves in their totality within unobstructed [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]. Huayan therefore says, “not one colour, not one fragrance is outside the middle way,” which accords in direction with Tiantai's “every colour and every fragrance possesses the three thousand.”

Relation to emptiness: the “non-duality” of the one true dharma-realm is continuous with the Prajñāpāramitā “emptiness,” but Huayan emphasises the affirmative side of “non-duality” (all is one), whereas the [[madhyamaka|emptiness school]] emphasises the apophatic side of “absence of own-nature.” This difference of emphasis is one of the principal distinctions between Huayan and Madhyamaka.

src.q: The similes of the [[one_true_dharmadhatu|one true dharma-realm]], Indra's net, and the ocean-seal samādhi.

src.t: Fazang, *Huayan Yisheng Jiaoyi Fenqi Zhang* and *Huayan Jin Shizi Zhang*
src.q: Using gold and the lion as similes to explain the [[one_true_dharmadhatu|one true dharma-realm]] and the six characteristics.

tt.fix: Chinese scholastic doctrine: Fazang and Chengguan in the Tang

name: Dharmadhātu Dependent Origination
desc:
All dharmas are mutually [[dependent_origination|dependent in origination]], mutually identical and mutually interpenetrating; one is all and all is one. It is the Huayan-style unfolding of the doctrine of dependent origination.

Its difference from Āgama dependent origination lies in the level of observation: Āgama dependent origination explains the arising and the cessation of suffering in terms of “origination” and “cessation,” within a soteriological framework; Huayan's dharmadhātu dependent origination explains the mutual containment of all dharmas from “the vision of one who has already become Buddha,” within a framework of the realised realm. Both are called dependent origination, but one answers “how is there suffering,” the other “how is there non-obstruction.”

“Mutual identity” (sameness) and “mutual interpenetration” (mutual containment) are the two basic relations of dharmadhātu dependent origination: mutual identity is spoken from the side of “substance” (one is all, so that without destroying the marks of difference the substance is one), and mutual interpenetration is spoken from the side of “function” (one enters many, many enter one, mutually containing without losing the marks of one and many). The [[ten_gates|ten mysterious gates]] explain these two relations from ten angles.

Zhiyan states plainly in the *Huayan Yisheng Shixuan Men*: “The whole *Avataṃsaka* sūtra's purport is a comprehensive elucidation of dharmadhātu dependent origination” — dharmadhātu dependent origination is Huayan's comprehensive summation of the one great sūtra.

src.q: “The whole *Avataṃsaka* sūtra's purport is a comprehensive elucidation of [[dharma_realm_origination|dharmadhātu dependent origination]].”
“With one Buddha-land filling the ten directions, the ten directions enter one without remainder, and the original marks of the world are not destroyed,” and so on.

name: The Four Dharma-Realm

src.q: “The aspects of the dharma-realm are essentially only three, yet taken together they comprise four: first, the dharma-realm of phenomena; second, the dharma-realm of principle; third, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena; fourth, the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon.”

src.t: Dushun, *Xiu Dafangguang Fo Huayan Fajie Guan Men*
src.q: The three contemplations: the contemplation of true emptiness, the contemplation of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena, and the contemplation of universal containment — the forerunners of the [[four_dharmadhatu|four dharma-realms]].

Chengguan's explanation: the contemplation of true emptiness is the dharma-realm of principle; the contemplation of the non-obstruction of principle and phenomena is as its name; the contemplation of universal containment is the dharma-realm of the non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon.

name: The Six Characteristics in Mutual Interfusion
desc:
The universal, the particular, the same, the different, the accomplished, and the destroyed. The six characteristics are mutually identical without obstructing one another, and are used to explain the relation between whole and part.

The six characteristics are divided into three pairs:
- The universal and the particular: one containing many qualities is the universal; the many qualities not being one is the particular. Thus a house is the universal, while the rafters, tiles, and so on are the particular;
- The same and the different: the many meanings not contradicting one another and together forming one whole is the same; the many meanings set against one another, each differing, is the different. Thus rafters and tiles differ in shape and kind (the different), yet together make the house (the same);
- The accomplished and the destroyed: that these meanings thereby form [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]] is the accomplished; that each meaning abides in its own dharma without moving is the destroyed. Thus if rafters and tiles each abide in their own nature the house is not made (the destroyed), whereas relying on dependent origination the house is made (the accomplished).

The key lies in “mutual interfusion”: the six characteristics are not a relation of succession but sixfold observation of one and the same thing — when the universal is spoken, all six are present; when the particular is spoken, all six are likewise present. This mode of analysis and the [[ten_gates|ten mysterious gates]] explain each other: the ten mysterious gates speak of the non-obstruction of phenomenon with phenomenon in terms of “relation,” while the six characteristics speak of it in terms of “structure.”

Source: the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, “The Ten Grounds” chapter, contains the names of the six characteristics; Vasubandhu's *Daśabhūmikasūtra-śāstra* explained them, and the Huayan school (Zhiyan, Fazang) developed them into the doctrine of “the six characteristics in mutual interfusion.”

src.t: *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Huayan Jing), “Chapter on the Ten Stages” (Shi Di Pin)
src.q: The first appearance of the names of the six characteristics.

name: Chan
desc:
Its basis is the thought of the Prajñāpāramitā and of [[tathagatagarbha|tathāgatagarbha]]. Its core is pointing directly to the human mind and [[seeing_nature|seeing one's nature and becoming Buddha]], with no-thought, no-mark, and no-abiding as its function. Its ultimate aim is to understand the mind and see the nature, and to realise thoroughly the original face.

The “direct pointing” of “pointing directly to the human mind” is the methodological key: without establishing stages of doctrine and contemplation, it points directly to the fact that the present single moment of mind is where the Buddha-nature manifests. This has a starting point similar to Tiantai's “beginning from the single moment of mind,” but Tiantai retains a complete sequence of doctrine and contemplation, whereas Chan abolishes stages and maintains “not establishing words and letters, a separate transmission outside the teachings.”

Its intellectual basis has two sources: the Prajñāpāramitā side of “non-attainment” and “non-abiding,” and the affirmative side of tathāgatagarbha in “seeing the nature.” The *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch*, “Chapter on Concentration and Wisdom,” summarises it under three headings — “no-thought as the cardinal principle, no-mark as the substance, non-abiding as the root” — which precisely encompasses both at once: no-thought and no-mark are the apophatic side of prajñā, while the “nature” that is “seen” is the affirmative side of tathāgatagarbha.

Lineage: Bodhidharma (came to China in the early 6th century) → Huike → Sengcan → Daoxin → Hongren → Huineng (638–713) — the Southern school became the mainstream. After Huineng it divided into the two lines of Nanyue Huairang and Qingyuan Xingsi, which gave rise to the five houses and seven schools (Linji, Guiyang, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan, plus Huanglong and Yangqi).

src.t: *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch* (Liuzu Tan Jing)
src.q: “No-thought as the cardinal principle, no-mark as the substance, non-abiding as the root”; “pointing directly to the human mind, [[seeing_nature|seeing one's nature and becoming Buddha]].”
The [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]] meaning of “seeing the nature” — the scriptural basis for Chan's “seeing one's nature and becoming Buddha.”
“One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere” — the line by which Huineng awakened to the way.

tt.form: Indian origins c. 5th century (Bodhidharma came to China in the early 6th century)
tt.fix: establishment of the school in China: Tang, Huineng (638–713)
tt.trans: the *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch* is a record of Huineng's teachings; the earliest extant version is the Dunhuang manuscript, and there are also the Huixin, Qisong, and Zongbao editions

name: Seeing One's Nature and Becoming Buddha
desc:
Pointing directly to the human mind, seeing one's own nature, one is in that moment no different from the Buddha.

“Nature” is the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]], the [[pure_mind|inherently pure mind]]. The doctrinal premise of “seeing one's nature and becoming Buddha” is the tathāgatagarbha tradition's “the mind-nature is originally pure, defiled by adventitious dust” — since the inherent nature just is Buddha, becoming Buddha is not acquiring something but seeing what is inherently possessed. “Seeing” is not a new act of cognition but knowledge in accordance with reality after the covering has been removed.

Chan therefore says “not establishing words and letters” while still preserving the *Platform Sūtra*, and says “no cultivation, no realisation” while still discussing stages of practice — this is not a contradiction but means that words and practice are both fingers pointing at the moon; to take the finger as the moon turns them into an obstacle instead.

Relation to the schools of the teachings: Chan raises “seeing the nature” to the status of cardinal principle, and therefore gives little weight to arrangements of doctrinal-classification ranking. This is often regarded as Chan's “supra-doctrinal” characteristic, and it made Chan another path in the Tang, when scholastic doctrine was elaborate.

src.t: *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch* (Liuzu Tan Jing)
src.q: “The self-nature of bodhi is originally pure; simply use this mind and directly accomplish Buddhahood.”
“Seeing the nature” and the meaning of the [[buddha_nature|Buddha-nature]].

tt.fix: the *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch*

name: No-thought, No-mark, and No-abiding
desc:
In thought yet without thought; in marks yet free of marks; not abiding in any dharma. This is the [[chan|Chan]] school's practical formulation of the Prajñāpāramitā samādhi.

The *[[doc_11|Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch]]*, “Chapter on Concentration and Wisdom”: “No-thought as the cardinal principle, no-mark as the substance, non-abiding as the root.” The meaning of the three:
- No-thought: it is not “having no thoughts,” but “in thought yet without thought” — in every moment of thought, no thought that can be clung to is seen;
- No-mark: it is not “not seeing marks,” but “in marks yet free of marks” — seeing all marks without attachment;
- Non-abiding: this is the inherent nature of a person — “in every moment not abiding in any dharma,” that is, not lingering over or grasping any dharma.

“Non-abiding” is the root of the three, directly continuous with the *Diamond Sūtra*'s “one should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.” Their relation is perfectly interfused: because there is no-thought, there is no-mark; because there is no-mark, there is non-abiding; and the three are at once the state of one mind.

Relation to the Sanlun school's “non-attainment”: both take “non-attachment” as their core, but Sanlun, by refuting the false, establishes no thesis of its own, while Chan takes “seeing the nature” as an affirmative goal — alike in one respect, different in another, which is precisely the result of the union of the Prajñāpāramitā and tathāgatagarbha traditions.

src.t: *Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch* (Liuzu Tan Jing), “Chapter on Concentration and Wisdom”
src.q: “No-thought as the cardinal principle, no-mark as the substance, non-abiding as the root.”
“One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere” — Kumārajīva's translation (c. 402).

tt.trans: the *Diamond Sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva under the Yao Qin (c. 402); the various editions of the *Platform Sūtra* took shape between roughly the 8th and 13th centuries

name: Pure Land
desc:
The school is founded on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*, the *Sūtra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*, and the *[[doc_19|Amitābha Sūtra]]*. Its core is [[faith_vow|faith and vows]] together with recitation of the name, and rebirth in the Pure Land. Its ultimate aim is rebirth in Sukhāvatī and non-retrogression to Buddhahood.

The doctrinal structure has three elements:
- Faith: faith in the power of Amitābha Buddha's vows (especially the eighteenth vow, “ten recitations and one is assured of birth”);
- Vows: the vow to be born in the land of Sukhāvatī;
- Practice: holding fast to the name (recitation of the Buddha's name), up to “single-mindedness undistracted.”

The relation to other-power is the Pure Land's distinguishing feature: it does not rely on self-power to cut off afflictions and realise the truth, but on the power of Amitābha's vows to receive and guide one to rebirth. This “easy path of practice” defines its relation to the other schools (the “difficult path of practice”) — Nāgārjuna's *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* distinguishes the “difficult path” and the “easy path,” and the Pure Land school based its doctrine of the “two paths and two powers” on this.

The foundations of Pure Land thought are karma and saṃsāra (the problem to be solved) and the bodhisattva path (the fruition of rebirth there — rebirth is not for enjoyment but for “non-retrogression to Buddhahood,” that is, for obtaining conditions of practice in which one no longer falls back).

Lineage: Huiyuan of Mount Lu (who formed the White Lotus Society in 402) → Tanluan → Daochuo → Shandao (613–681, who brought it to completion); thereafter the masters of the Song and Ming and, in modern times, Yinguang.

src.q: Amitābha Buddha's forty-eight vows, especially the eighteenth vow.
The sixteen contemplations and the nine grades of rebirth.
Holding fast to the name and single-mindedness undistracted.

src.t: Shandao, *Guanjing Sitie Shu* (Four-Part Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra)
src.q: The establishment of the school's doctrine of “ordinary beings entering the reward land” and of “single-minded exclusive recitation.”

tt.form: c. 1st–2nd century (composition of the Pure Land scriptures)
tt.fix: establishment of the school in China: Tang, brought to completion by Shandao (613–681)
tt.trans: the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* and the *Amitābha Sūtra* were translated between the Eastern Han and the Cao Wei; the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra* was translated by Kālayaśas under the Liu Song (424); the *Guanjing Sitie Shu* was composed by Shandao in the Tang

name: Faith and Vows
desc:
The core of the [[pureland|Pure Land]] school: faith in the power of Amitābha's vows, and the vow to be born in Sukhāvatī.

The content of “faith” in the *[[doc_19|Amitābha Sūtra]]* is faith that “the sentient beings of that land have none of the many sufferings but experience only various pleasures,” and faith that “holding fast to the name with single-mindedness undistracted, one attains rebirth”; the “vows” are the actual aspiration to be born in that land. The two, together with “practice” (recitation of the name), are called the three requisites of “faith, vows, and practice.”

Shandao's *Guanjing Sitie Shu* particularly emphasises “the two kinds of deep faith, concerning the practitioner and the dharma”: deep faith that one is oneself an ordinary being of sin and birth-and-death (deep faith concerning the practitioner), and deep faith that Amitābha's forty-eight vows will certainly receive and guide one (deep faith concerning the dharma). This structure of “two kinds of deep faith” is the theoretical formulation of the Pure Land school's “other-power” position — it does not abolish practice but redefines practice as “accepting in faith” and “reciting the name.”

src.q: “If there be a good man or good woman who hears of Amitābha Buddha and holds fast to the name ...”

src.t: Shandao, *Guanjing Sitie Shu* (Four-Part Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra)
src.q: The two kinds of deep faith, concerning the practitioner and the dharma.

tt.fix: Shandao in the Tang (613–681)

name: Recitation of the Buddha's Name
desc:
The practice of the [[pureland|Pure Land]] school: holding fast to the name, with single-mindedness undistracted.

There are four forms of Buddha-recitation: recitation of true reality, contemplative recitation, recitation before an image, and recitation of the name. The Pure Land school (especially the line of Shandao) adopts the single gate of recitation of the name, because it “covers all three capacities” — it can be practised by the wise and the dull alike.

There are two readings of “single-mindedness undistracted”: “single mind” can be understood as “concentration without distraction” (single mind in the phenomenal sense) and as “accord with [[suchness|suchness]]” (single mind in the principle sense). The line of Shandao emphasises the former, while Tiantai and Chan commentators after the Song adopted both, and this is the main point of divergence in interpretation within the Pure Land tradition.

src.q: “Holding fast to the name, whether for one day ... or for seven days, with single-mindedness undistracted.”
In the lowest grade of the lowest birth, “because he recites the Buddha's name.”

src.t: Shandao, *Guanjing Sitie Shu* (Four-Part Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra)
src.q: “Single-mindedly and exclusively mindful of Amitābha's name.”

tt.fix: Shandao in the Tang established the single gate of recitation of the name as the primary practice of the Pure Land school

name: Vinaya
desc:
The school is founded on the *[[doc_25|Dharmaguptaka Vinaya]]* and the *[[doc_26|Brahmajāla Sūtra]]*. Its core is taking the precepts as teacher and strictly upholding the monastic rules. Its ultimate aim is that from the precepts concentration arises, from concentration wisdom is produced, and one becomes Buddha and saves sentient beings.

Its distinctive feature is “taking the precepts as an independent course of study”: most other schools treat the precepts as a foundation, whereas the Vinaya school makes the study and observance of the monastic rules themselves the basis of its foundation as a school. Daoxuan (596–667), taking the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* as his basis, analysed it into four divisions — the dharma of the precepts, the essence of the precepts, the practice of the precepts, and the marks of the precepts — and judged the *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* to be “the precepts of the perfect teaching,” that is, pervaded by the Mahāyāna; hence “the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya pervades the Mahāyāna” became the central tenet of the Nanshan Vinaya school.

Classification of the precepts (according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā* and other vinaya treatises): **precepts by nature** are those wrong in themselves, not requiring a rule to be laid down (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying and so on); **precepts of prohibition** are those not wrong in themselves, laid down to protect the former (not drinking alcohol, for instance). This distinction shows that within the precepts there are two kinds, “essential” and “protective,” of differing weight.

Daoxuan's *Sifenlü Shanfan Bique Xingshi Chao* is one of the three major works of the Nanshan school and became the standard basis for the precepts in Chinese Buddhism.

src.q: Translated by Buddhayaśas and Zhu Fonian under the Yao Qin — the extensive Vinaya in general use in China.

src.t: Daoxuan, *Manual of Practice: Abridging the Profuse and Supplying the Omissions of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya* (Sifen lu shanfan buque xingshi chao)
src.q: The four divisions of the [[jie_ti|dharma of the precepts]], the essence of the precepts, the practice of the precepts, and the marks of the precepts, together with the judgment that “the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya pervades the Mahāyāna.”
The scriptural basis for the Mahāyāna bodhisattva precepts.
